thread.title: The Future Of Banking: How Industry Changes Will Disrupt The Banking Norms

author: Orlando Vega
title: The Future Of Banking: How Industry Changes Will Disrupt The Banking Norms
text:
Overview
This article looks to address the wide variety of challenges that the banking industry is facing and what the leaders of the industry must do to face these challenges. The banking industry is facing many new issues with competition coming from unlikely sources, technology driving away traditional banking, and the GOP-led Congress looking to rid themselves of parts of the Dodd Frank act that was passed during the last financial crisis. These issues are at the forefront of a new era for banking that will help separate the top institutions from the rest.
Banking Reform
Ever since the 2008 financial crisis, the United States government has increased regulations and oversight of the banking industry. The increased compliance costs have hurt the bottom line of many banks and placed a large competitive strain on local and regional sized banks. The CEO of Utah’s regional-sized Zions Bank testified before a congressional committee that he had to hire about 27 new employees strictly for the purpose of ensuring the compliance of all the new banking regulations. However, despite the increased costs and regulations, banks are enjoying record profit numbers as shown in their quarterly earnings reports. Large banks such as JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Bank of America ( BAC ), and Citigroup ( C ) have already reported strong earnings and beating analyst expectations. Analysts expect this trend to continue with the tax cuts and increasing interest rates elevating expectations for the industry as a whole. According to Zachs.com , major banks on the S&P 500 have reported a 30.8% year-over-year earnings growth in 2018 Q1. Additionally, banks as a whole have reported profits of $56 billion in 2018 Q1, up 27.7% compared to Q1 2017. Despite these numbers, banks are still looking to roll back many of these Obama-era regulations that they say are still hampering their ability to help more consumers.
This week, Congress approved a bill that would loosen some of the regulations put in place during the financial crisis. The area that Dodd-Frank reform will have the most important impact will be with local and regional banks such as BB&T ( BBT ), Zion Bank ( ZION ), and others of similar size. A key part of the bill was that the government raised the threshold in which banks would be subject to the strictest forms of regulation from $50 billion to $250 billion in assets. This will lower the amount of banks faced with additional regulations from 38 to 12 due to the new rules. Smaller banks will now have the ability to take more risks and face less regulatory scrutiny as a result of the new bill. However, many people fear that this lessened regulation will have a domino effect that will result in consolidation of smaller banks by merging with larger companies. Time will tell if these new laws will promote pro-growth or threaten the possibly of another financial crisis similar to a decade ago.
Technological Changes
New technology has continuously rolled out in the financial industry over the last few years. Mobile banking through computers and smartphones have been increasingly popular and now those platforms are held to high standards for banks who want to be competitive with consumers. People are able to do things with technology that was not possibly years ago such as sending money electronically. Electronic payment services such as Zelle, Paypal and Venmo are facing increasing competition to be able to transfer money between people quickly and forcing the banking industry to provide new products capable of this. Additionally, another popular service that banks now offer is mobile depositing in which clients can deposit checks right through their smartphones. These new technological changes are forcing banks to reconsider their strategies. This has led many people to start predicting the demise of bank branches.
As shown in the graph below, banks have been closing more and more of their physical branch locations as of late. Banking in physical locations is increasingly becoming a thing of the past as the younger generations prefer convenience through technology instead of going to a local branch. As a result, large banks are starting to close the doors on these locations due to high operating costs and a decline in the benefits. Bank of America ( BAC ), Wells Fargo ( WFC ) and JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) have closed over 500 branches combined between 2012 to 2016. Overall, more branches are closing in the US today then are opening in a trend similar to the “retail apocalypse” that is happening in the retail industry.
New Competition
Recently, the banking industry has become more susceptible to other large companies looking to gain a market share in the industry. Amazon ( AMZN ), a perennial industry innovator, has been talking recently about expanding into financial services. Much like with their purchase of Whole Foods, they are seen as a company who can come in and disrupt the status quo of an industry. With their new services such as Amazon Pay and Amazon Cash, they are able to bring a wide array of new offerings to their base of over 100 million Prime subscribers. Furthermore, a recently featured CNN Money article describes how Silicon Valley is going after the finance industry and looking at entering the market. In addition to Amazon, Apple ( OTC:APPL ) recently partnered with Goldman Sachs ( GS ) on a joint credit card that will promote Apple Pay. Facebook has also been exploring ways to create their own cryptocurrency that can be used to make payments through their social media platform.
Despite all these new ideas by large technology companies, the banking industry still does not see these ventures as a serious threat to their businesses. This is due to the high regulations and barriers to entry that banks have been opposed to for many years now. The compliance costs, equity needed, and regulations make it nearly impossible for these already large companies to enter the industry. The CNN Money article views these companies as more of a threat to the payment processing companies such as Visa ( V ), Discover ( DFS ), and MasterCard ( MA ) due to their partnerships they are creating with large banks for their payment services. As a result, banks must be mindful of the new competition, but investors should have no cause for concern right now.
Conclusion
Banking as a whole must be able to identify the changes coming to their industry and properly address any changes that must be implemented in order to alleviate the concerns of investors. At the moment, banking regulations are being loosened and giving banks the ability to earn more profits. However, the potential of a recession as well as the midterm elections loom over what regulations will be put in place to ensure the safety of consumers. Additionally, new technology is forcing banks to evolve and offer new services to become more attractive to the younger generation of banking clients. From mobile deposit to Zelle, banking services are looking to focus on convenience for the clients and threatening to close physical locations throughout the U.S. Finally, competition from Silicon Valley will force the industry to evolve in order to fight off outsider threats. However, high barriers to entry will keep the industry giants safe as long as they adapt to the new climate of the market.
